content: 1. Caruso et al. This tool was designed to capture the unique challenges faced by women in accessing safe and dignified sanitation. The study was published in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. 2. In another study, Caruso et al. (2017b) explored and defined sanitation insecurity by examining women’s gendered experiences of urination, defecation, and menstruation in rural Odisha, India. This research highlighted the significant impact of inadequate sanitation on women’s daily lives and health. The findings were published in BMJ Global Health. 3. Cavill, Chambers, and Vernon (2015) reviewed the sustainability of Community-Led Total Sanitation (CLTS) programs, emphasizing the importance of maintaining open defecation-free (ODF) communities. Their insights were published in the Frontiers of CLTS: Innovations and Insights series by the Institute of Development Studies (IDS). 4. Clasen et al. This study, published in Environmental Science & Technology, provided a practical tool for evaluating the effectiveness of sanitation programs. 5. Coffey et al. (2014) investigated the preference for open defecation in India, revealing cultural and social factors that influence sanitation behaviors. Their findings were published in the Economic and Political Weekly. 6. Cole (2015) combined sanitation marketing with participatory approaches to sustain ODF communities in Malawi. This approach was documented in UNICEF’s Eastern and Southern Africa Sanitation and Hygiene Learning Series. 7. Cronin et al. (2017) examined the equity implications of sanitation interventions based on recent health and nutrition evidence. Their study, published in the International Journal for Equity in Health, highlighted the need for inclusive sanitation programs. 8. Curtis, Danquah, and Aunger (2009) conducted a review of hygiene behavior across 11 countries, identifying factors that motivate planned and habitual hygiene practices. Their findings were published in Health Education Research. 9. De Buck et al. (2017) conducted a systematic review of handwashing and sanitation behavior change interventions in lowand middle-income countries. This mixed-method review, published by the International Initiative for Impact Evaluation (3ie), provided evidence-based recommendations for improving sanitation practices. 10. Devine (2009) introduced the Sanitation FOAM framework, which analyzes sanitation behaviors to design effective programs. This framework was developed under the World Bank’s Water and Sanitation Program. 11. Dreibelbis et al. (2015) developed a multidimensional scale to assess attitudinal determinants of sanitation uptake and use. This tool, published in Environmental Science & Technology, aids in understanding the factors influencing sanitation adoption. 12. Dreibelbis et al. (2016) demonstrated the effectiveness of nudging handwashing behaviors among primary school students in Bangladesh without direct behavior change communication. Their study was published in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. 13. Dreibelbis et al. (2013) proposed the Integrated Behavioral Model for Water, Sanitation, and Hygiene (WASH), a framework for designing and evaluating behavior change interventions in resource-limited settings. This systematic review was published in BMC Public Health. 14. The World Health Organization (WHO) guidelines on sanitation and health emphasize the critical role of sanitation in controlling microbial hazards, including bacteria, viruses, protozoa, and helminths. These guidelines outline the transmission pathways of pathogens and the importance of safe sanitation systems in reducing disease risks. 15. Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a growing global health threat, as identified by the WHO. Poor sanitation contributes to the spread of AMR by facilitating the transmission of resistant pathogens through contaminated water, soil, and food. Safe sanitation systems and hygiene practices are essential barriers to prevent AMR transmission. 16. Pathogens such as bacteria, viruses, protozoa, and helminths are transmitted through various pathways, including contaminated water, food, and surfaces. Effective sanitation interventions aim to interrupt these pathways and reduce the risk of infection. 17. Unsafe disposal of human excreta, including open defecation, can facilitate the breeding of disease vectors such as flies and mosquitoes. These vectors mechanically transport pathogens, increasing the risk of disease transmission. Safe sanitation systems must address these risks by containing excreta and preventing vector breeding. 18. Specific pathogens, such as Campylobacter spp., Clostridium difficile, and Salmonella enterica serovar Typhi, are associated with significant health risks, including diarrhea, typhoid fever, and systemic infections. Sanitation interventions play a crucial role in controlling these pathogens by reducing their transmission pathways. 19. The WHO guidelines highlight the importance of sanitation in controlling soil-transmitted helminths (STH) and other excreta-related pathogens. 20. Research underscores the importance of integrating sanitation, hygiene, and water interventions to reduce the burden of diseases such as diarrhea, trachoma, and mosquito-borne illnesses. Safe sanitation systems are critical for improving public health outcomes in low-income settings.
